questions.stem:
A car dealer offers purchasers a three year warranty on a new car. He sells two models, the Zippy and the Nifty. For the first 50 cars sold of each model the number of claims under the warranty is shown in the table below.

$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}\hline & \text{Claim} & \text{No claim}\\ \hline \text{Zippy} & 35 & 15\\ \hline \text{Nifty} & 40 & 10\\ \hline\end{array}$

One of the purchasers is chosen at random. Let $A$ be the event that no claim is made by the purchaser under the warranty and $B$ the event that the car purchased is a Nifty.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Given that the purchaser chosen does not make a claim under the warranty,
(c) find the probability that the car purchased is a Zippy.
(2)

parts.label: d
parts.text:
(d) Show that making a claim is not independent of the make of the car purchased.

Comment on this result.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(d) $\mathrm{P}(A' \cap B) = 0.4$; $\mathrm{P}(A')\mathrm{P}(B) = 0.75 \times 0.5 = 0.375$ M1
Since $\mathrm{P}(A' \cap B) \neq \mathrm{P}(A')\mathrm{P}(B) \Rightarrow$ not independent A1
One of models is less reliable A1 (3)

questions.question_text:
A car dealer offers purchasers a three year warranty on a new car. He sells two models, the Zippy and the Nifty. For the first 50 cars sold of each model the number of claims under the warranty is shown in the table below.

$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}\hline & \text{Claim} & \text{No claim}\\ \hline \text{Zippy} & 35 & 15\\ \hline \text{Nifty} & 40 & 10\\ \hline\end{array}$

One of the purchasers is chosen at random. Let $A$ be the event that no claim is made by the purchaser under the warranty and $B$ the event that the car purchased is a Nifty.
(a) Find $\mathrm{P}(A \cap B)$.
(2)
(b) Find $\mathrm{P}(A')$.
(2)
Given that the purchaser chosen does not make a claim under the warranty,
(c) find the probability that the car purchased is a Zippy.
(2)
(d) Show that making a claim is not independent of the make of the car purchased.

Comment on this result.
(3)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) $\mathrm{P}(A \cap B) = \frac{10}{100} = \frac{1}{10} = 0.1$ M1 A1 (2)
(b) $\mathrm{P}(A') = \frac{75}{100} = 0.75$ M1 A1 (2)
(c) $\mathrm{P}(B'|A) = \frac{\mathrm{P}(B' \cap A)}{\mathrm{P}(A)} = \frac{\frac{15}{100}}{\frac{25}{100}} = \frac{15}{25} = \frac{3}{5} = 0.6$ M1 A1 (2)
(d) $\mathrm{P}(A' \cap B) = 0.4$; $\mathrm{P}(A')\mathrm{P}(B) = 0.75 \times 0.5 = 0.375$ M1
Since $\mathrm{P}(A' \cap B) \neq \mathrm{P}(A')\mathrm{P}(B) \Rightarrow$ not independent A1
One of models is less reliable A1 (3)

questions.stem: A drinks machine dispenses coffee into cups. A sign on the machine indicates that each cup contains 50 ml of coffee. The machine actually dispenses a mean amount of 55 ml per cup and 10% of the cups contain less than the amount stated on the sign. Assuming that the amount of coffee dispensed into each cup is normally distributed find

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) the standard deviation of the amount of coffee dispensed per cup in ml,
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
Let $X$ represent amount dispersed into cups
$X \sim \mathrm{N}(55, \sigma)$
(a) $\mathrm{P}(X<50) = 0.10 \Rightarrow \frac{50-55}{\sigma} = -1.2816$ M1 B1
$\sigma = 3.90137$ M1 A1 (4)

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) the percentage of cups that contain more than 61 ml.
(3)

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Following complaints, the owners of the machine make adjustments. Only 2.5% of cups now contain less than 50 ml. The standard deviation of the amount dispensed is reduced to 3 ml.

Assuming that the amount of coffee dispensed is still normally distributed,

(c) find the new mean amount of coffee per cup.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
Let $Y$ represent new amount dispensed.
$Y \sim \mathrm{N}(\mu, 3)$
(c) $\mathrm{P}(Y<50) = 0.025 \Rightarrow \frac{50-\mu}{3} = -1.96$ M1 B1
$\mu = 55.88$ M1 A1 (4)

Assuming that the amount of coffee dispensed is still normally distributed,

(c) find the new mean amount of coffee per cup.
(4)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
Let $X$ represent amount dispersed into cups
$X \sim \mathrm{N}(55, \sigma)$
(a) $\mathrm{P}(X<50) = 0.10 \Rightarrow \frac{50-55}{\sigma} = -1.2816$ M1 B1
$\sigma = 3.90137$ M1 A1 (4)
(b) $\mathrm{P}(X>61) = \mathrm{P}(Z> \frac{61-55}{3.90137...})$ M1
$= \mathrm{P}(Z>1.54)$ A1
$= 1 - 0.90382 = 0.0618$; 6.18% A1 (3)
Let $Y$ represent new amount dispensed.
$Y \sim \mathrm{N}(\mu, 3)$
(c) $\mathrm{P}(Y<50) = 0.025 \Rightarrow \frac{50-\mu}{3} = -1.96$ M1 B1

questions.stem:
A restaurant owner is concerned about the amount of time customers have to wait before being served. He collects data on the waiting times, to the nearest minute, of 20 customers. These data are listed below.

15, 14, 16, 15, 17, 16, 15, 14, 15, 16,
17, 16, 15, 14, 16, 17, 15, 25, 18, 16

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Find the median and inter-quartile range of the waiting times.
(5)

parts.label: b
parts.text:
An outlier is an observation that falls either $1.5 \times$ (inter-quartile range) above the upper quartile or $1.5 \times$ (inter-quartile range) below the lower quartile.

(b) Draw a boxplot to represent these data, clearly indicating any outliers.
(7)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) $1.5 \times \mathrm{IQR} = 1.5 \times 1.5 = 2.25$ M1 A1
$Q_1 - 1.5 \times \mathrm{IQR} = 12.75 \Rightarrow$ no outliers below $Q_1$ A1
$Q_3 + 1.5 \times \mathrm{IQR} = 18.75 \Rightarrow 25$ is an outlier A1
Boxplot, label scale M1
14, 15, 16, 16.5, 18.75 (18) A1
Outlier A1 (7)

parts.label: c
parts.text:
(c) Find the mean of these data.
(2)

parts.label: d
parts.text:
(d) Comment on the skewness of these data.  Justify your answer.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(d) Almost symmetrical/slight negative skew B1
Mean (16.1) $\approx$ Median (16) and $Q_3-Q_2$ (0.5) $\approx Q_2-Q_1$ (1.0) B1 (2)
